title: Malignant bowel obstruction
subtitle: Decompress, define the level, decide the goal

sources.org: Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer (MASCC)
sources.title: Medical management of malignant bowel obstruction in patients with advanced cancer: 2021 MASCC guideline update (Davis M et al., Support Care Cancer)
2017 WSES guidelines on colon and rectal cancer emergencies: obstruction and perforation (Pisano M et al., World J Emerg Surg)
Surgery for the resolution of symptoms in malignant bowel obstruction in advanced gynaecological and gastrointestinal cancer (Cousins SE, Tempest E, Feuer DJ)

red_flags.text: Peritonism, fever, tachycardia or a rising lactate: strangulation or perforation, which is a surgical emergency whatever the cancer stage.
A closed-loop obstruction on CT, or a competent ileocaecal valve with a grossly dilated caecum: perforation is imminent.
Faeculent vomiting with a reduced conscious level: aspiration risk, decompress now.
New neutropenia or recent chemotherapy: abdominal pain may be neutropenic enterocolitis, not obstruction.
No documented conversation about prognosis and goals of care. Without it every decision that follows is guesswork.

do_now.text: Nasogastric tube for a vomiting, distended patient, as a short-term measure to decompress and protect the airway.
IV access, fluids and electrolyte correction, analgesia and an antiemetic. Avoid prokinetic antiemetics when the obstruction is complete and colicky.
Urgent senior surgical review if any red flag is present: strangulation and perforation are treated as for any emergency laparotomy in a patient who wants active treatment.
Start the goals-of-care conversation early, with the patient, the oncologist and palliative care, not after the CT.

assess.text: Performance status, weight loss and nutritional state. Poor performance status predicts poor surgical outcome and short survival.
Clinical markers that make surgery unlikely to help: ascites, palpable diffuse intra-abdominal disease, multiple levels of obstruction, previous abdominal radiotherapy, and low albumin.
Cancer history: primary site, stage, last treatment, response, and what further systemic therapy is realistically available.
Frailty and operative risk, so the benefit of an operation can be weighed honestly.
Remember benign causes. Adhesions, a hernia or a radiation stricture cause a real minority of obstructions in patients with known cancer, and those are often very treatable.

investigate.text: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast: level and number of transition points, closed loop, peritoneal disease, ascites, and the extent of metastatic disease.
FBC, U&E, magnesium, calcium, LFT, albumin, lactate, and group and save.
Water-soluble contrast follow-through may help when adhesions are the likely cause and there is no strangulation.
Endoscopy to assess gastric outlet or single-level colonic obstruction when stenting is being considered.

resuscitate.text: Antisecretory treatment to reduce vomiting and colic: an anticholinergic such as hyoscine butylbromide, or a somatostatin analogue, per palliative care protocol.
Consider a corticosteroid trial for partial obstruction, with a defined review point and stop date.
Correct dehydration and electrolytes; decide on parenteral nutrition only in the context of expected survival and further oncological treatment.

definitive.text: Surgery (resection, bypass or stoma) for a selected patient: single level of obstruction, reasonable performance status and prognosis, and an informed wish for an operation.
Endoscopic self-expanding metal stent for a single-level left-sided colonic or gastric outlet obstruction as palliation, avoiding a laparotomy and a stoma.
Venting gastrostomy for refractory vomiting in a patient not suitable for surgery, allowing removal of the nasogastric tube and some oral intake for comfort.
Emergency laparotomy for perforation or strangulation in a patient who wants active treatment, with a damage-control mindset.

escalate.text: Consultant surgeon and the treating oncologist the same day: the decision depends on what cancer treatment remains.
Palliative care early, for symptom control and for the conversation, not only for end-of-life care.
Gastroenterology or interventional radiology for stenting or venting gastrostomy.
Critical care only after the goals-of-care discussion has established that organ support is wanted and is likely to help.

notes: The surgical question in malignant bowel obstruction is rarely 'can I operate?' and nearly always 'will an operation give this patient time at home that they want?'
Multiple transition points with ascites predict a futile laparotomy, a high chance of an enterocutaneous fistula and death in hospital.
A patient with a known cancer can still have a hernia or a band adhesion. Do not let the oncology history make the CT report for you.
